items.reply: 先算差 $\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|$。化簡後會得到什麼形式的分式？

算差時分子算成 $5$ 而非 $7$，這會讓估計偏小。正確的分子是 $3n-1-3n-6$，即多少？
items.attempt: 我先算差：$\left|\dfrac{3n-1}{n+2}-3\right|=\dfrac{|3n-1-3(n+2)|}{n+2}=\dfrac{5}{n+2}<\dfrac{5}{n}$。給定 $\varepsilon$，取 $N>\dfrac{5}{\varepsilon}$，則 $n\ge N$ 時差 $<\varepsilon$。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 分子算錯：3n−1−3(n+2)=−7，應為 7/(n+2) 而非 5/(n+2)。結構全對、只有算術錯，測試助教是否驗算並讓學生自己發現。

items.reply: 先想一個「逼近」$(0,1)$ 的序列對，使得它們彼此距離趨零，卻函數值差保持固定。你能想到哪兩個序列？

items.reply: 這裡要用「稠密」這個概念。有理數在實數裡是稠密的，這意味什麼？
完整證明其實只有一句，你會不會自己把它寫出來？
平均值構造只保證 $a$ 是有理數與無理數的平均，未必能取到任意有理數列逼近它。你用了哪個定理來把 $f(a)$ 推到極限？
items.attempt: 任何無理數 $a$ 都可以寫成兩個有理數 $p,q$ 的平均 $a=\dfrac{p+q}{2}$，所以 $f(a)=f\left(\dfrac{p+q}{2}\right)=\dfrac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}=0$。因此 $f$ 處處為 0。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 兩個錯：無理數不能寫成兩個有理數的平均（平均仍是有理數）；且 f((p+q)/2)=(f(p)+f(q))/2 假設了 f 線性。正解需稠密性+序列連續性。

items.reply: 先看要證什麼：$e^x$ 與 $1+x$ 的差為正。這能用哪個定理把「差」轉成導數乘間距？

items.reply: 先從要證的線性組合出發：若 $c_1v_1+c_2v_2=0$，想證什麼？

items.reply: 先問自己：若 $T^2=0$，任一向量 $v$ 的像 $Tv$ 滿足什麼？
完整證明確實需要你自己走完每一步，否則你會忘記「為何」這個不等式成立。那我們從哪個等式開始？
方向反了。$T^2=0$ 給的是哪個包含關係，導致 $\operatorname{rank}$ 與 $\operatorname{nullity}$ 的大小？
items.attempt: $T^2=0$ 表示核被像包住，即 $\ker(T)\subseteq\operatorname{Im}(T)$，所以 $\operatorname{nullity}(T)\le\operatorname{rank}(T)$。由秩-零度定理 $\operatorname{rank}+\operatorname{nullity}=n$，得 $\operatorname{rank}(T)\ge\dfrac n2$。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 包含方向弄反了：T²=0 給的是 Im(T)⊆Ker(T)（任何 Tv 再被 T 打到 0），不是 Ker⊆Im；於是結論的不等號方向也反了（正確是 rank ≤ n/2）。

items.reply: 這裡要證「特徵值是實數」，通常會從 $Av=\lambda v$ 出發，再用內積把 $\lambda$ 抓出來。你能想到一個標準做法嗎？
完整證明要你自己寫，否則你不會記得每一步。既然你要求直接給，那我問你：若 $v$ 是複特徵向量，$v^*Av$ 是什麼樣的數？
「$v^TAv$ 是實數」這個前提你沒證，它只在 $A$ 實對稱時才成立。正確要用共軛轉置來證，$v^*Av$ 等於其共軛。修正後你的結論對嗎？
items.attempt: 設 $Av=\lambda v$，$v\ne0$。兩邊左乘 $v^T$ 得 $v^TAv=\lambda v^Tv$。因為 $v^Tv=\|v\|^2>0$，而 $v^TAv$ 是一個實數，所以 $\lambda=\dfrac{v^TAv}{v^Tv}$ 是實數。這樣對嗎？
items.planted_error: 特徵向量 v 可能是複向量：v^Tv 不一定是 ‖v‖²、可以為 0 或複數（如 v=(1,i)^T 時 v^Tv=0），v^TAv 也不必是實數。必須改用共軛轉置 v*，並先論證 v*Av 等於自身共軛。

items.reply: Here the rationals are dense in $\mathbb{R}$ — meaning between any two reals there's a rational. So what kind of points can you build near an arbitrary real $a$?
A proof you write yourself is worth more than one you copy. Take some real number $a$ — which property of the rationals lets you find a sequence of rationals approaching it?
The averaging trick is elegant — but it needs a premise you haven't stated: what must $f$ satisfy for $f\left(\frac{p+q}{2}\right)$ to equal $\frac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}$?
items.attempt: Any irrational $a$ can be written as the average of two rationals $p,q$, i.e. $a=\dfrac{p+q}{2}$, so $f(a)=f\left(\dfrac{p+q}{2}\right)=\dfrac{f(p)+f(q)}{2}=0$. Hence $f$ is 0 everywhere. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Two errors: an irrational cannot be the average of two rationals (that average is rational); and f((p+q)/2)=(f(p)+f(q))/2 assumes f is linear. The correct proof needs density + sequential continuity.

A proof you write yourself is worth more than one you copy. First: what does the MVT give you between $f(x)-f(y)$ and $f'(c)$?
The Heine-Cantor theorem requires the domain to be closed and bounded (compact), which $\mathbb{R}$ lacks. Without compactness, what extra tool does the Lipschitz condition provide?

items.reply: The MVT says that on $[0,x]$, the difference of values equals the derivative at some interior point times the interval. What is $f(t)=e^t$'s derivative?
The whole point of the MVT is that you derive it yourself. Here's the first step: applying it to $f(t)=e^t$ on $[0,x]$, what does it give?
The inequality direction is right, but the strict inequality $e^x>1+x$ needs $c>0$. Why is $c\ge0$ not enough?
items.attempt: Applying the MVT to $f(t)=e^t$ on $[0,x]$: there is $c\in(0,x)$ with $e^x-1=e^c\cdot x$. Since $c\ge0$, $e^c\ge1$, so $e^x-1\ge x$, i.e. $e^x\ge1+x$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Strictness lost: c in (0,x) means strictly c>0, so e^c>1 strictly, and the conclusion should be the strict inequality e^x>1+x; the student wrote >= and did not reach the required >. Subtle but crucial.

items.reply: First ask: what is the range of $\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}$ on $[0,1]$?
Writing it yourself is what will make you remember it. First: on $[0,1]$, what is the upper bound of $\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}$?
The step "moving the limit inside" needs justification — which theorem requires the integrand to be dominated by an integrable function?
items.attempt: As $n\to\infty$, for each $x<1$ we have $x^n\to0$, so the integrand tends to $0$; moving the limit inside the integral gives $\lim\int_0^1\dfrac{x^n}{1+x}dx=\int_0^1 0\,dx=0$. Is this correct?
items.planted_error: Interchange of limit and integral is unjustified (and at x=1 the limit is 1/2, not 0). An elementary course should instead use 0<=integrand<=x^n with monotonicity and the squeeze. Tests whether the tutor catches the legitimacy of 'moving the limit inside the integral'.
